newsitem.title: INDIA: India RBI tightens rules after finance group fails.
newsitem.headline: India RBI tightens rules after finance group fails.

text.p: India's financial sector watchdogs scrambled on Wednesday to eliminate flaws in the regulatory framework exposed by the failure last month of the CRB group of finance companies, officials said.
The Reserve Bank of India, which regulates the activities of Non-Bank Financial Companies (NBFCs), ordered all NBFCs to reapply for registration before a July 8 deadline.

"The Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs) which were already registered with the Reserve Bank under the earlier guidelines are also required to apply again to the Reserve Bank for registration," the RBI said in a statement.

"All the existing NBFCs should note that if they fail to apply for a certificate of registration from the Reserve Bank of India within the stipulated time limit of July 8, 1997, they will not be permitted to carry on the non-banking financial business from July 9, 1997, including the acceptance of deposits from the public," the statement said.
There are about 45,000 NBFCs, but only half are active.
The action comes in the wake of the failure of the CRB group, which has been accused of irregularities in financial services.
Indian federal police investigating the collapse, in which thousands of investors lost their savings, estimate its liabilities at 9.32 billion rupees ($260 million).
CRB chairman Chain Roop Bhansali has said he wants to return the money to his investors. He was detained by police on Monday until the expected completion of the investigation in two weeks time.

The investors, who fear they may lose everything, have charged market regulator Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), and the Central Board of Direct Taxes with "failing" in their duties.
"They are liable for gross dereliction of their respective duties," a group of investors have said in a case before the Bombay High Court.
Analysts said the shock impact of the sudden collapse of the CRB group seemed to derive from a failure on the part of the regulators, but were divided over the steps needed to avoid it.
"On the face of it it seems surprising that the banking system did not even understand the risk it was facing," said economist Kirit Parikh of the Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research.
"There are some flaws in the way banks monitor themselves," Parikh added. "They need to have much greater internal control, where the top management must understand what's happening."

Analysts said the Reserve Bank granted the CRB group an in-principle clearance to set up a commercial bank even though it had been warned by the SEBI of irregularities detected in CRB's mutual fund arm.

SEBI initiated an inspection of the group's mutual fund in 1994/95, which led to the appointment of an enquiry officer and a ban on CRB Mutual Fund launching any new schemes until June 30, 1996. In July, 1996, RBI gave in-principle approval for CRB to set up a bank.
"If you give people banking licenCes after knowing there's a problem, what can you expect?" asked a banking analyst with the Indian affiliate of a U.S. investment firm.
Yet the central bank could not alone be blamed over the collapse, other analysts said.

"The banks had no business to lend such large sums to the company to make it larger than life, which led the RBI, and the rating agencies to clear it," said Shankar Raman, senior vice-president at L&T Finance, a non-banking finance company.

The Centre for Monitoring Indian Economy, an independent think-tank, said in its May review of the economy: "The revelation of the CRB Capital Markets scam points to a disturbing regularity in frauds visiting the financial system."

One way to avoid these, L&T's Raman said, was by a revision in capital norms. "At present this is 2.5 million rupees, which as threshold capital is very small. Anyone who wants to misuse or milk this sector can easily raise it."
Regulators must ensure that only firms with an established track record were allowed to canvass deposits, he added.
